description: Every note type in the Sparrow vault. The sf tool validates against this file, the app renders boards and forms from it, and Templates/ is generated from it. Change a type here and nowhere else.

conventions.links: Obsidian wiki links in quotes, "[[Name]]". The name must match the target note's title or name exactly.

scopes.vault: folder is relative to the vault root
scopes.book: folder is relative to Series/<Series>/Books/<N Title>/

conventions.enum: either the name of a status set below, or a literal list of values
conventions.computed: filled by the tool, never by hand
conventions.extraProperties: a type with extraProperties true accepts properties it does not list (System/Config.md uses this for its settings)
conventions.extends: a note with an extends property is a book delta of a series note and holds only what differs
conventions.secrets: twists and hidden facts go in a > [!secret] callout in the body; packets withhold them unless a scene's reveal list names the note. A callout titled with a scene (> [!secret] Book 1, S-039) is revealed by that scene and known in every packet after it
conventions.first_seen: where a bible note first appears on the page, as Book 1, S-005; packets for earlier scenes leave the note out
conventions.later: an inbox idea tagged later is one Kyle put aside on the Ideas board to come back to; its status stays inbox. Keep and drop on the board set status keep or discard, the decided time and any reason in decision_note; nothing is moved or deleted
conventions.accepted: Kyle accepts a scene card on the Chapter Grid; the app sets accepted to the time he tapped. Needs work removes accepted and puts his reason in decision_note. Beats and conflicts are kept or dropped on their boards the way ideas are, and market notes (market case, comps, keyword sets, titles) on the Market board
conventions.scene_title: A scene card's title is a one-line summary of what happens in the scene (Kyle, 2026-10-17, T-009), such as "Grey turns down the guild's offer". Agents write titles that way and read them as the scene's summary. The file name follows the title (S-012 <title>.md); Kyle changes it from Edit card in the app, which renames the file.
conventions.regenerate: Rewrite on a board sets a proposal's status to regenerate, the decided time, and what Kyle wants changed in decision_note. The agent that owns the note rewrites it from that note and sets it back to inbox
conventions.headline: a scene's headline is one sentence saying what happens, shown as its header in the app. The team writes it from the prose when it is empty (System/Tools/jobs.mjs makes a summaries job); Kyle may change it, and the team never rewrites a headline that is filled in
conventions.timed: A timed list item starts with the scene it becomes true at, as "B2 S-024: Terrakinesis: moves soil and stone by will". Packets show an item only once that scene has happened, and the Book Index shows each one with its scene, so a want or a power that changes from act to act keeps its history. An item with no scene is always true.
conventions.open: open lists what Kyle has not decided yet about a note, one question per line. Agents ask Kyle or flag it rather than settle it on the page.

common.description: Properties every type accepts. created and updated are dates; updated is computed.

series.description: A series. Every book lives inside one, even a series of one.
series.body: What the series is about, the series-level story question, and notes that hold across books.

book.description: One book. Its shape (length, chapters, framework) is a setting here, never a design constant.

publish_date.description: The day Kyle plans to publish the book, set on its Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

editing_pass.description: The editing pass under way, as the app names it ("Draft 3: changes", named by the draft being made); the app sets it when a pass begins (Kyle, 2026-11-07).

editing_pass_start.description: The day the editing pass under way began. The publish estimate times the pass from here, so earlier editing work does not slow its pace.

editing_pass_base.description: How many of the book's changes were already decided when the editing pass under way began, so the pass's percent counts only its own changes. Set by the app (Kyle, 2026-11-12).

draft2_end.description: The day draft 2 was finished (the developmental and line edit done). Set by the app when the next pass begins.

draft3_end.description: The day draft 3 was finished (the proofreads done). Set by the app when the next pass begins.

publish_estimate.description: The app's estimated publish day from the stage dates, written when it moves by more than three days; the daily mailbox check passes changes to the Chief of Staff (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

market_start.description: The day market research started for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

market_end.description: The day market research finished for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

market_paused.description: Days during market research when the book sat waiting (for example while Kyle worked on another book). Taken off the days the stage took (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

planning_start.description: The day planning started for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

planning_end.description: The day planning finished for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

planning_paused.description: Days during planning when the book sat waiting (for example while Kyle worked on another book). Taken off the days the stage took (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

outlining_start.description: The day outlining (outline and beats) started for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

outlining_end.description: The day outlining (outline and beats) finished for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

outlining_paused.description: Days during outlining when the book sat waiting (for example while Kyle worked on another book). Taken off the days the stage took (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

writing_start.description: The day writing draft 1 started for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

writing_end.description: The day writing draft 1 finished for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

writing_paused.description: Days during writing draft 1 when the book sat waiting (for example while Kyle worked on another book). Taken off the days the stage took (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

editing_start.description: The day editing (drafts 2 to 4) started for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

editing_end.description: The day editing (drafts 2 to 4) finished for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

editing_paused.description: Days during editing when the book sat waiting (for example while Kyle worked on another book). Taken off the days the stage took (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

publishing_start.description: The day publishing started for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

publishing_end.description: The day publishing finished for this book. The app fills it in as the book moves on; Kyle can change it on the Overview (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

publishing_paused.description: Days during publishing when the book sat waiting (for example while Kyle worked on another book). Taken off the days the stage took (Kyle, 2026-11-06).

rewrite_done.description: The chapters Kyle has been through in the app's Rewrite tab (Done with this chapter, 2026-11-05). When every rewritten chapter is listed, the app saves the next draft.

book.body: Pitch, synopsis and working notes for the book.

book-spec.description: The single input to one-shot mode. Status inbox until Kyle keeps it.
book-spec.body: Anything the one-shot run must know that the properties do not hold.

market-thesis.description: A niche drilldown ending in a one-paragraph thesis.
market-thesis.body: The thesis paragraph, then the evidence from the exports with file names and dates.

comp.description: A comparable title doing the exact thing. A comp is proof, not inspiration.
comp.body: Notes on what the comp proves and where each number came from.

keyword-set.description: Seven KDP keywords, three categories and the promises the book must deliver.
keyword-set.body: Where each keyword came from (the search terms and export).

title-candidate.description: A title, subtitle and series name, tested against the comps.
title-candidate.body: Why the title signals the niche, and how it reads next to each comp.

cover-brief.description: The brief for the cover artist. Covers are per book.
cover-brief.body: The brief as sent, must-haves, must-avoids, and a dated feedback log of every round of notes.

cover-comps.description: The comp cover board for the artist.
cover-comps.body: One section per comp cover, with the image embedded from Cover/Comps/.

cover-iteration.description: One round of art from the cover artist.

idea.description: Any proposal: premise, Big Issue, opinion, twist, editorial note. Kyle keeps, regenerates or discards.

reasons.description: One-press reasons Kyle gave with Keep, Later or Drop. They teach the team his taste.

round.description: The brainstorm round the idea came from (1 blind pitch, 2 response, 3 fusion), so the keep rate per round shows if later rounds earn their cost.

step.description: The workflow step (System/Workflow.md) this result belongs to, as its number ("18"), or the name of a step of Kyle's own. Results of one step are that step's store; the app's Workflow mode reads them.

origin.description: Where a workflow result came from: made by the team, brought in by Kyle from elsewhere, or written by Kyle in the app.

panel_score.description: The judging panel's score, 1 to 5, for a workflow result; Kyle decides.

panel_note.description: The panel's one line on why it scored the result so.

checked.description: When Kyle said a kept result still holds after an earlier step changed (Workflow mode's Still fine).

idea.body: Three sections: ## The idea, ## Why it could work, ## Risks / costs.

character.description: Series canon for a character. A book delta (with extends) holds only what differs in one book.

arc_points.description: The character's arc scene by scene, as "S-012: 4": 0 is fully in the Lie, 10 fully living the Truth (Character Arcs).

arc_draft.description: True while arc_points are the team's guess and Kyle has not changed or confirmed them.

wants.description: What the character wants, timed (conventions.timed): one line each time it changes, as "B2 S-040: lean on the village". The latest one before a scene is the want at that scene.

looks.description: Face, build and usual clothes, timed: "B1 S-001: white Platinum robes on subscription, bandage around his temples".

abilities.description: Powers, skills, stats and penalties, timed: "B2 S-024: Terrakinesis: moves soil by will". A lost power gets its own line saying so.

open.description: What Kyle has not decided about this character (conventions.open).

character.body: Who they are, how they sound, relationships in detail. Secrets go in a > [!secret] callout.

place.description: A place in the series world.

open.description: What Kyle has not decided about this note (conventions.open).

place.body: Description and history. Secrets go in a > [!secret] callout.

lore.description: A rule, system or piece of history in the series world.

open.description: What Kyle has not decided about this note (conventions.open).

lore.body: The full rule and its consequences. Secrets go in a > [!secret] callout.

item.description: Gear, artefacts, loot: what people carry and trade.

open.description: What Kyle has not decided about this note (conventions.open).

item.body: Description, stats, history. Secrets go in a > [!secret] callout.

thread.description: A plot thread with its own dramatic question.

open.description: What Kyle has not decided about this note (conventions.open).

thread.body: How the thread runs across the book or series. Secrets go in a > [!secret] callout.

progression.description: A state change at a point in the manuscript. Replaces hand-kept state in Story So Far.

beat.description: A structural beat in the book's framework, with the scenes that deliver it.
beat.body: What happens in the beat and why it sits here.

conflict.description: A collision from one of the three conflict sources, run for three cause-and-effect beats.
conflict.body: The collision in full, beat by beat.

scene.description: A scene card in the properties and the prose in the body.

chapter_id.description: The chapter's own ID, which never changes when chapters are added, moved or deleted (CH-007). Every scene of a chapter carries the same one; a chapter note with one belongs to that chapter wherever it now sits, and its `chapter` number is then only a label. Handed out by the app and by System/Tools/chapter-ids.mjs; never typed by hand.

threads.description: Story threads this scene moves (Plot Grid).

day.description: Story day the scene happens on, counting from day 1 (Timeline).

tension.description: How tense the scene is, 1 to 10 (Tension and Pacing).

outcome.description: How the point-of-view character's goal turns out: yes, yes-but, no, no-and.

mood.description: How the scene feels, from -5 (dark) to 5 (bright) (story shape).

card_draft.description: Card fields the team filled in that Kyle has not confirmed yet (the app shows them as the team's guess until he changes or confirms them).

scene.body: The prose, or for a planned scene the card notes.

promise.description: A setup the reader is owed a payoff for.
promise.body: What was promised and how it will pay off.

theme.body: How the theme is dramatised, never stated.

previously.description: What a finished book changed in the series. The next book's agents read every one.
previously.body: What changed in series canon, open threads at the end, and the cast state table.

session.description: The record of one substantial thread: who took part, what was decided.
session.body: One ## Round heading per round, voices as > [!voice] callouts, then ## Kyle's decisions and ## Reflection.

note.description: A standing instruction from Kyle to the team. Agents handle open notes first.

recipe.description: A standing instruction of Kyle's in plain English, used by name ("draft chapter 4 with the cliffhanger recipe"). Any agent that is handed a recipe follows it on top of its usual rules.

use_for.description: What it is for, in a few words (a chapter end, a stat block).

decision.description: One decision about a book, with who made it and why. Studio-wide decisions go in the Decision Ledger instead.
decision.body: The decision, the options weighed, and what would change it.

research.body: The findings, each tied to a source in the list or marked unverified.

task.description: A piece of work with an owner. Studio and system to-dos live in the vault's Tasks/ (the nightly validate files its problems there). A book's to-dos live in that book's Tasks/ and are about its pages: `chapter` (and `scene`) say where, and `generated: true` marks one the team found in a check rather than one Kyle wrote. The writing screen shows a chapter's to-dos beside the page.

context.description: Which part of Kyle's work it belongs to, for the To-do map: writing (the books' pages and stories), publishing (KDP, Vellum, covers, editions), marketing (market research, blurbs, keywords, launch), sparrow (the app), team (the AI team and workflow), admin (setup, computers, keys, upkeep). A book's to-dos are writing when left out (Kyle, 2026-11-01).

priority.description: need: something that has to get done. want: something Kyle would like to do when there is time (Kyle, 2026-11-01).

chapter.description: Book to-dos: the chapter it is about.

chapter_id.description: The ID of the chapter this belongs to (see scene.chapter_id).

scene.description: Book to-dos: the scene it is about, when it is about one.

generated.description: True when the team wrote it after a check; Kyle's own to-dos leave it out.

found_by.description: For a generated to-do: the check that found it (continuity, plot, character, line, genre).

done_note.description: When the team marks a to-do done: one line on what in the text fixed it, so Kyle can reopen it if he disagrees.

task.body: What needs doing and how to tell it is done.

report.description: A note from one Sparrow agent up the line (Kyle, 2026-11-01): the agents report to Sparrow, the coordinator, and Crow reports to the Story Specialist. Mailbox/<to>/ holds the notes for one reader, named "YYYY-MM-DD HHMM from <sender>, <topic>". Notes are never edited or deleted: a reply is a new note in the sender's folder with re naming the note it answers, and the reader logs what it has read in that folder's READ.log. The `report-up` skill has the how.

title.description: "YYYY-MM-DD HHMM from <sender>, <short topic>", the time in UTC, so the folder sorts oldest first.

from.description: The agent or program that wrote it: Writer, Story Specialist, Contrarian, Market Analyst, Developmental Editor, Line Editor, Beta Reader, Continuity Keeper, Crow, Sparrow.

to.description: Who reads it, the same as its folder: Sparrow, or Story Specialist for Crow's notes, or the agent a reply goes back to.

sent.description: When it was written, in UTC, like 2026-11-01T14:35Z.

needs.description: answer: a question for the reader. action: something for the reader to do or pass on, such as a to-do for Kyle. FYI: nothing to do.

re.description: In a reply: the title of the note it answers.

refs.description: What it is about: task ids (T-114), job ids (J-031), idea ids or vault paths.

report.body: A few plain sentences: what happened or what is needed, and what the reader should do. Kyle's words quoted as he wrote them.

writing-day.description: Kyle's Pomodoros on one day, written by the app's timer: how many he finished, the minutes and the words written during them, every word he typed that day (`typed`) and the minutes he spent typing (`typing_minutes`). Lives in Writing Log/ at the vault root, one note per day.

minutes.description: Minutes of work Pomodoros, including ones stopped early.

words.description: Words written during them, stopped ones included. Cuts are not taken away, so rewriting a passage counts the new words (Kyle, 2026-10-20).

typed.description: Words Kyle typed in the app that day, with or without a Pomodoro. Cuts are not taken away, and words the team puts on the page (filled brackets, Options, lines merged in from elsewhere) never count, so deleting them does not lower it either (Kyle, 2026-10-21).

typing_minutes.description: Minutes Kyle spent typing in the app that day, to one decimal place. The clock runs only while he types or changes the words on the page, and a gap of more than two minutes with nothing typed counts nothing, so time spent away or reading does not count (Kyle, 2026-10-29). Words an hour = typed / typing_minutes x 60.

writing-day.body: ## Pomodoros: one line per Pomodoro, `- HH:MM, N minutes, W words (S-012, S-013)`, with `(stopped early)` after the minutes for one stopped before its time (it adds minutes and words, not to pomodoros), oldest first. The app appends lines and never rewrites earlier ones.

style-guide.description: The book's voice rules. Overrides the default prose rules.
style-guide.body: The voice in plain words, with short approved examples.

timeline.description: Every step of the book with its time (Kyle, 2026-11-06: "I want you to be really granular with this. I want you to keep timestamps for like every step of the process ... it's the agent's responsibility to manage and track this stuff based on conversations and based on Sparrow app usage"). Append-only, oldest first. Agents add a line when Kyle or they start or finish a step; System/Tools/timeline.mjs adds the app's work from the vault's history. The six stage boundaries also go on Book.md as <stage>_start and <stage>_end.
timeline.body: One line per event, oldest first: `- <YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MMZ>[ to <HH:MMZ>] · <stage> · <what happened> · <who>`. Stage is market, planning, outlining, writing, editing or publishing. Who is Kyle, an agent's name, or app. Never edit or delete a line; a correction is a new line that says so.

updated.description: The last commit timeline.mjs read, so the next run starts after it.

story-so-far.description: The rolling summary the Writer reads before drafting.
story-so-far.body: What has happened so far, chapter by chapter.

book-index.description: One page per book that every agent reads first to look up a fact: the plan by act, every chapter in a line, and each character's wants, looks and abilities with the scene they start at. Built by `sf index`, never by hand.
book-index.body: Generated. Change the notes it points to, then run sf index.

braindump.description: Anything Kyle wants the team to know, in any order.
braindump.body: Free text from Kyle. Agents read it; they never edit it.

scene-notes.description: A scene's planning notes, kept beside its prose so the writing screen shows only the story: Kyle's outline, the team's notes and questions, and where the scene came from. One note per scene; the writing screen shows it under the scene's card.

scene.description: The scene these notes are about.

title.description: The scene's title, so the file is easy to find.

chapter_id.description: The ID of the chapter this belongs to (see scene.chapter_id).

scene-notes.body: Callouts as they stood in the scene: Kyle's outline, Team notes (bible proposals and continuity questions), Open for Kyle questions and Source lines. Agents add new team notes here, not in the prose.

chapter-beats.description: A chapter's beats: the moves of the chapter, each a short title and a one-line summary, kept beside the prose so the scenes hold only the story. The app shows the chapter by its beats, each opening to its prose, and Kyle edits beats and prose there.

chapter.description: The chapter these beats belong to.

chapter_id.description: The ID of the chapter this belongs to (see scene.chapter_id).

chapter-beats.body: One `## ` heading per beat, in reading order: the beat's title. Under it, the one-line summary, then `Starts: S-NNN · <first words>`: the scene the beat sits in and the first ten words of the paragraph it starts at, copied exactly without * or = marks. A beat with no prose yet has `Starts: S-NNN` and no words. Never put beats in the scene files. See `.claude/skills/chapter-beats/SKILL.md`.

chapter-plan.description: Kyle's plan for a chapter, as many paragraphs as he likes, kept beside the prose so the scenes hold only the story. The writing screen shows it in the right-hand column (the Plan tab) and Kyle writes it there.

chapter.description: The chapter this plan is for.

chapter_id.description: The ID of the chapter this belongs to (see scene.chapter_id).

chapter-plan.body: Kyle's words, free text. Agents read it whenever they work on the chapter (sf packet includes it) and never edit it.

chapter-scrap.description: Words Kyle cut from a chapter and loose notes he wants to keep out of the story, one scrap per chapter. The writing screen shows it in the right-hand column (the Scrap tab); Kyle writes it there or moves picked words into it from the page.

chapter.description: The chapter this scrap belongs to.

chapter_id.description: The ID of the chapter this belongs to (see scene.chapter_id).

chapter-scrap.body: Kyle's words, free text: cut lines and spare notes. Agents leave it alone and do not treat it as canon or as a plan; read it only when Kyle asks.

chapter-changes.description: The team's changes to one chapter of Kyle's draft (workflow step 39): each change quotes his exact words, gives the new words and the reason, and waits for his Keep or No in the app's writing screen, as Word's track changes do. The scene files are never rewritten by the team in editing; only Kyle's Keep puts a change in.

chapter.description: The chapter these changes belong to.

chapter_id.description: The ID of the chapter this belongs to (see scene.chapter_id).

draft.description: The draft the changes make: 2 when they change draft 1.

step.description: The workflow step that made them ("39" revise, "40" checks, "42" proofread).

touched.description: The share of the chapter's words the changes touch, in percent, as the Writer reported it.

chapter-changes.body: Optional lines before the first change (the Writer's report: share touched, questions). Then one `## C-NN` heading per change, in reading order, with the kind after a dot (`## C-03 · story`). Kinds: small (typo, punctuation, a continuity or tic fix: offered with Keep all), line (a sentence made better), story (from a story call or a chapter problem), new (mostly new words: read slowly). Under it, these lines: `Scene: S-NNN`, `Why: <the reason, naming the note, call or Style Guide rule>`, `Kyle: open` (the app sets kept, other, no or mine), any `Reply:` lines (Kyle's reply to the Writer on that card, written by the app; the Writer answers each with a new card, job kind `reply`), a card made from a reply also has `Re: C-NN` naming the card it answers, then `Was:` followed by Kyle's exact words as `> ` lines (copied from the scene file with its * and = marks, long enough to be found once; never empty: to add words, quote the sentence before and repeat it in Now), `Now:` followed by the new words as `> ` lines (none to cut), and for a new passage `Or:` with a second version as `> ` lines. See `.claude/skills/revise-as-changes/SKILL.md`.

draft.description: A saved draft of a book: a copy of every scene as it stood when Kyle started editing (Draft 1) or started the next draft, kept in the book's `Drafts/Draft N/` folder beside this note. The copies are never changed; tools and the app skip the Drafts folder except to show and export a draft. The scene files are always the draft being worked on.

note.description: Kyle's words about this draft, if any.

draft.body: One line saying which draft it is and when it was saved. The scene copies sit in the folder `Drafts/Draft N/` next to this note, each with the same file name it had in `Scenes/`.

chapter-titles.description: Chapter title options for the book, picked in the app (Kyle, 2026-10-29): the team offers four titles per chapter a round; Kyle ticks the one he likes or None of these, and the next round adds four more only for the chapters marked None, keeping the picked ones.

round.description: How many rounds of options the team has offered.

source.description: The agent that wrote the options.

chapter-titles.body: One `## Chapter N` heading per chapter, in order. Under it `Was: <the chapter's name before the first round>`, a blank line, then one `- [ ] <title>` line per option (the app ticks the one Kyle picks as `- [x]`, and only one per chapter), and last `- [ ] None of these`. A new round adds four option lines above None of these, only in chapters where None of these is ticked, and unticks it. Options are never removed. Picking a title in the app also renames the chapter (its scenes' chapter_title); unticking puts the Was name back.

book-matter.description: A book's front and back matter for the Kindle file (Kyle, 2026-11-04, replacing Vellum): the copyright page, dedication, also-by list, the next-book line, newsletter offer, about the author and the like. One note per book. The title page and the contents are made from the book itself and need no section.

source.description: Who wrote the first version (Kyle, or an agent).

book-matter.body: One `## Front: <page name>` or `## Back: <page name>` heading per page, in reading order: front pages come before chapter 1, back pages after the last chapter. Under it the page's words as plain prose; web links as [words](https://...). Pages named Copyright, Dedication or Epigraph show without a heading. Text above the first heading is a note to the team and is left out of the book.

knowledge.description: A craft note in the Library. Shelves are subfolders.
knowledge.body: The craft knowledge, with the framework or source named.

persona.description: A reader persona the Beta Reader reads as.
persona.body: Who this reader is, what they love, what makes them stop reading, how they report.

system-doc.description: Documentation and system notes: Docs/, System/, Taste/.

job.description: A request for an agent to do one piece of work, made from the app or a thread. GitHub runs requested jobs (.github/workflows/agent-jobs.yml) and the runner updates the note as it goes. Lives in Jobs/ at the vault root.

taken.description: The answers of this job Kyle has already used in the app, by name (B1, B2 for the braces of a fill job; all for the job as a whole, as when he picks one of its options or puts them away). The app writes it (2026-11-12), so his iPad and desktop never use an answer twice. Agents leave it alone.

job.body: ## Ask holds Kyle's words. The runner appends ## Result. For kind chat, thread names the conversation (a scene ID or chat-NNN) and the app shows every job in that thread in order. For kind fill, the ask lists the {braces} asks Kyle left in a scene (### B1, B2 ...) and the ## Result answers each under the same heading; the app puts the answers into the page and the agent never edits the scene.
job.kinds_about: THE ONE LIST OF JOB KINDS (2026-11-12, step 4 of the code structure redesign). The app and the runner (System/Tools/jobs.mjs) both read `kinds`; nothing else defines a kind. For each kind: `label` is what the app calls it in Kyle's words; `title` the job's title when he gives none (<<what>> is the target and its name; `title_without` when there is none); `agent` who runs it (the commit trailer); `ask` the ## Ask the app writes when the kind has fixed instructions (<<target>>; <<words|target>> is his words, or the target when he typed none; then `ask_with_words` when Kyle typed something, <<words>>, or `ask_without_words` when he did not); `steps` the lines the runner tells the agent, between Kyle's ask and the rules every run gets (<<target>>, <<target|what to say when there is none>>, <<job>> the job's ID; a line that reads differently with and without a target is written both ways). A kind with no `steps` gets `custom`'s. `chat` is put together by the runner itself, because it carries the conversation so far. A NEW KIND is one entry here and its name in the `kind` list below; the tests (System/Tools/tests/jobs.test.js) fail if the two lists differ, and hold every kind's steps to a kept copy.

If the chapter has prose, find the beats in it as it stands: each beat starts at a paragraph, and its Starts line names the scene and copies the first words of that paragraph exactly. Never change the prose. If the chapter has no prose yet, plan its beats from what Kyle says the chapter should do, each with a Starts line naming the scene it belongs in and no words. The beats go in the book's `Chapter Beats/` note for that chapter. Never change a scene's prose; an old beats note goes to the book's Archive first, never deleted.

fill.label: Fill braces
steps: Do this: Kyle is writing <<target>> in the app right now and left asks in {braces} in it for the team. Answer each one listed in the ask (### B1, ### B2 ...) as the Writer (`.claude/agents/writer.md`), in his voice. Square brackets in his text are his own (System screens, tags like [Deserter]): never treat them as an ask, never change them (Kyle, 2026-10-23). Read `Taste/Style Fingerprint.md`, the book's `Style Guide.md`, the scene note for <<target>> (it may be a little behind his page; the Paragraph lines in the ask are what he has now), the scene's notes in `Scene Notes/` and the chapter's plan in `Chapter Plans/` if there is one.

- A **gap** (Kind: gap) is a hole in a sentence, like "she was wearing {...}". Write only the words that replace the marker so the sentence reads on, in the prose's tense and point of view. No quotes, no explanation.

- An **ask** (Kind: ask) is a question or an instruction, like "{how was she dressed}" or "{research: make this farmerly}". Answer it as prose that can sit in the scene as a new paragraph right below Kyle's (his braces stay above it until he deletes them): one paragraph unless the ask wants more. When the ask needs real-world knowledge (how a trampled squash plant looks, how a video like that is made), first think it through as a researcher: what would actually be there, and how the point-of-view character would name it (a farmer's words for a farmer). Use web search when you are not sure. Never invent a fact; a detail you are not sure of stays out.

- Write plain text in the page's own style, set out the way Kyle's prose around the ask is: no `>` quote arrows, no headings, no lists, no code blocks (Kyle, 2026-10-19: "I don't like the arrows"). *Italics* and **bold** only where his pages use them.

- When the ask wants text from an earlier book or scene and there is more than one version, read the lines just before the ask and pick the version they point to (Kyle, 2026-10-19). Copy it word for word in that book's own layout, and say in `result` which scene you took it from and what other versions exist. J-010: "Poppy said 'Inspect this dirt.' Grey inspected the dirt" points to the plain "Dirt" box (B1 S-003), not "Bucket of Dirt" (B1 S-011); the bucket only comes after the bracket.
- Follow the prose rules in CLAUDE.md and `.claude/skills/anti-slop/SKILL.md`. Run `System/Tools/sf lint` on your answers if they are longer than a few lines.
- Never edit the scene file or any other note: the app puts your words into Kyle's page itself. Your answers go only in the job note.

- The `## Result` section is exactly one `### B<n>` heading per ask, the same names as in the ask, each followed by your words and nothing else (no "Kind:", no commentary). Set `result` to one sentence such as "Filled 2 asks in <<target>>." If you cannot answer one, leave its heading out and say why in `result`.

combine.title: Combine <<what>>

forge.label: Forge a new specialist
forge.title: Forge a new specialist: <<what>>
forge.ask: Kyle wants a new specialist on the team: <<words|target>>. Forge it the way Writers Room's /forge did. First research a knowledge folder for the field in `Library/` (a few sourced notes: every fact names its source or is marked unverified; never invent one). Then write the agent as `.claude/agents/<name>.md` in the house style of the other agent files (name, description, `team:` line, `skills:` list, what it must and must not do), with an empty MEMORY.md and Journal.md in `.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`, and say in the Result how it differs from the agents the team has. steps: Do this: forge the new specialist named in the ask, as the coordinator, in three steps.

- Research: follow `.claude/skills/study/SKILL.md` to build a knowledge folder `Library/<Topic>/` (type `knowledge`, one note per subject, with an `_Index.md`). Use web search. Every real-world fact names its source (title and link); a claim you could not source is marked "(unverified)". Never invent a source, quote or figure. Five to ten notes is enough; cover what the book will actually put on the page.

- Agent: write `.claude/agents/<kebab-name>.md` in the same format as the existing agent files (front matter `name`, `description`, `team:` line, `tools`, `model: inherit`, `memory: project`, `skills:` list of existing skills it should load; then "What you are for", "How you work" naming its `Library/<Topic>/` folder, "Never", "Reporting and files"). It advises and checks; it never writes prose or changes canon. Start its description with "Awaiting Kyle's approval." and create `.claude/agent-memory/<kebab-name>/MEMORY.md` empty.

- Approval: file a studio to-do in the vault's `Tasks/` (ID from `System/Tools/sf next-id task`; `status: open`, `owner: Kyle`) titled "Approve the new <Name> specialist", whose body says in three lines what it knows, when the team would call it, and that deleting nothing is needed to refuse it (the agent file moves to `Archive/` with a note). Add one line to the Roster in CLAUDE.md only after Kyle approves, never in this job.

workflow-step.label: A workflow step
steps: Do this: run <<target|the workflow step named in the ask>> of `System/Workflow.md` for this book, as the coordinator, exactly as that step's row says: the agents in its Who column, as many minds as its Minds column (separate, blind contexts where it says so), the inputs in its Needs column, and the skills it names. A judging step follows `.claude/skills/judge-panel/SKILL.md`. Read CLAUDE.md "How the team runs" first; never more than four agents on the job.

- What earlier steps decided is in the book's `Ideas/` folder: idea notes with a `step` property are workflow results, and the ones with `status: keep` are what Kyle kept at that step. Use the kept results of earlier steps as the step's inputs, and its own kept results too when the ask is to change or add to them.

- Workers: each mind in the Minds column is its own helper (Agent tool), briefed with the step's question, the paths in its Needs column, Kyle's words and the output you want, under 300 words back; you read only the step row and what you must pass on, never the helpers' inputs. Helpers that turn kept material into a list (traits, dramatic elements, minor characters, chapter beats from kept summaries) run on effort `medium`; brainstorms, test drives, outlines, prose and judges keep full effort. Never more helpers than the row asks for.

- File every new result as one inbox idea note in the book's `Ideas/` folder, all of them in one step with `node System/Tools/jobs.mjs ideas .scratch/<<job>>-ideas.json` (`status: inbox`, `step` set to the step number as a string, `origin: team`, `source` the agent or lens that made it, a fitting `kind`, `target` a wiki link to the character or note it is about, or "Chapter N", when there is one). Title: the result itself in a few words; `pitch`: one or two sentences. A list step (twenty traits) is one note per item.

- When the ask is to judge, do not file new ideas: score each inbox result of the step(s) named, writing only `panel_score` (1 to 5) and `panel_note` (one line, naming the reason) on those notes, all in one step with `node System/Tools/jobs.mjs score .scratch/<<job>>-scores.json`, and put the panel's recommendation in the Result. Never set `keep`, `discard` or `later`: Kyle decides.
- When the ask carries Kyle's note on a result to change, file the changed version as a new inbox result with `related` linking the old one; never edit the old one.
- Never change a kept note, canon or prose. In the Result, say in plain words how many results were filed or scored, and the two or three strongest with one line each.

revise.label: Changes for this chapter
revise.title: Changes for <<what>>

Follow only the story calls he kept. Never edit a scene file.
steps: Do this: follow `.claude/skills/revise-as-changes/SKILL.md` as the Writer (`.claude/agents/writer.md`) for <<target|the chapter named in the ask>> of this book (workflow step 39; the whole process is `.claude/skills/edit-book/SKILL.md`). Before any new words, read the codex: the series `Characters/` and `Lore/` notes, the places, items and threads the chapter touches, the book's `Story So Far.md` and the `Book Index.md` entries of the people in the scene, and check every fact a new line states against them; a fact no note supports goes in a { } question, never in the text. Every open to-do for the chapter in the book's `Tasks/` gets a change whose Why starts `To-do T-NNN:`. Kyle's notes in the text ({ } asks, and plain lowercase [ ] notes in older books) are instructions: each becomes a change that carries it out, and every change that answers a { } ask carries two different options, the second under `Or:` (Kyle, 2026-11-12). Write the chapter's changes as one `chapter-changes` note in the book's `Changes/` folder: each change quotes Kyle's exact words, gives the new words and its reason, and new passages carry a second version. Kyle's sentence stays unless a kept story call, a chapter problem, a Style Guide rule or plain sense gives a reason. Never edit a scene file: Kyle keeps or refuses each change in the app. If the chapter already has a changes note with changes Kyle has not decided, stop and say so in the Result.

reply.label: A new card from your reply
reply.title: New card from your reply on <<what>>
reply.ask: Kyle replied on a change card in <<target>> of this book, to tell the Writer why he made a choice. Make a new card from his reply, following the `reply` steps.
steps: Do this: Kyle replied on one or more cards in the changes note of <<target|the chapter named in the ask>> of this book (`Changes/Chapter N changes.md`), to tell you why he made a choice (Kyle, 2026-11-12: "i need to be able to reply within the changes, to explain to the writer why i made a choice, and for the writer to create a new card based on my reply"). Each reply is a `Reply:` line under that card, in his words. Work as the Writer (`.claude/agents/writer.md`), following `.claude/skills/revise-as-changes/SKILL.md` for the format, the leash and "Know the world first".

- Answer every reply in the note that no card answers yet (a card answers a reply when it has `Re: C-NN` for that card and its `Asked:` line is that reply), the one the ask names first. For each, read the card he replied on, what he chose on it (its `Kyle:` line: kept, other, no, mine or still open) and the scene file as it stands now: if he accepted the card, the page has its new words.

- His reason is the rule for that spot. Make one new card that does what his reply asks or explains: if he says why he kept his own words, never offer his old words back changed the same way; if he says what was wrong with the card, offer a version without that fault. If his reply asks for the same thing at more spots in the chapter, one card per spot. If he asks for options, or the right answer is unclear, add a second version under `Or:`. A question back to him goes in a { } note inside the Now. Your new card replaces the card he replied on: while that card is still open, the app retires it as soon as your card is in the note (Kyle, 2026-11-12: "Once the writer makes a new card, shouldn't the writer scrap the old card ... the writer can include the other stuff that's not mentioned in the old card if they want to"). So the new card covers the whole spot the old one did: carry over every part of the old card that his reply does not object to (other fixes in the same words, a repeated word, a typo), and leave out only what he objected to.

- Each new card goes at the end of the note with the next free C number, in the existing card format: `## C-NN · kind`, then `Scene: S-NNN`, `Why: Your reply on C-NN`, `Re: C-NN`, `Asked:` his reply word for word on one line, `Change:` what this card does with his reason in one or two plain sentences, `Kyle: open`, then `Was:` copied exactly from the scene file as it is now (with its * and == marks, long enough to occur once) and `Now:`. Never change, move or remove another card, and never touch a `Kyle:` or `Reply:` line. Never edit a scene file.

- Then add a dated entry to `.claude/agent-memory/writer/Journal.md`: the card he replied on, his reason in his own words, and the lesson it carries for your next pass. In the Result, one plain sentence per reply: which card you made and what it does.

study.description: A finished story Kyle is studying in Crow (the character and plot study app): how its author builds characters and plot. Lives at Studies/<Title>/Study.md. Its notes are analysis, never canon for Kyle's books.

source.description: What Kyle shared it from. The story's text itself is never saved here; only summaries and short quotes.

study.body: ## Plot structure (how the story is built so far) and ## What we are learning (running conclusions about character and plot).

study-character.description: One character of a studied story: the card in Crow (the character and plot study app). Its picture, if Kyle added one, is Studies/<Study>/Faces/<name>.jpg.

facts.description: The card's key lines, at most six

best_lens.description: The character lens that explains this character best so far

study-character.body: One ## section per character lens, named as the lens note, with - Field: value lines; then ## Checks (one '- <Lens> · <Field>: SC-001 yes; SC-002 partly; ...' line per checked field, verdicts yes, partly, no, not shown: does the card's reading hold in each scene); then ## Notes.

study-scene.description: One scene of a studied story, read for character and for plot.

where.description: Where it sits in the book, as Volume 1, Chapter 2

characters.description: Names of the study's characters in the scene

summary.description: One or two sentences, in our words

premise.description: The scene's premise in one line: the situation the scene starts from, as a what-if (Kyle, 2026-10-27)

source_url.description: Where Kyle can read the scene in full (the translator's page); the text itself is never saved here

study-scene.body: ## Plot with - Driver, - Link (therefore, but, and then), - Why next, - Best lens, - Why, - Others (non-carded forces and their roles, as The world (opposes)) lines; ### Beats (one '- <Who> (<kind>[, turning][, ki|shō|ten|ketsu]): <beat>' line per beat, Who being the character or force that causes it, and the last tag the kishōtenketsu part the beat belongs to); ### Retelling (the scene in our words, one paragraph); then one ### section per plot lens. Then one ## section per character with - Best lens, - Why, - Holds (yes, partly, no, first), - Role (driver, opposes, supports, receives), ### Moments (short quotes, each with what it shows) and one ### section per character lens.

study-lens.description: A way of reading a character or a plot in Crow (the character and plot study app). Studies/Lenses/<name>.md. A new lens is a new note; the app shows it without a change.

framework.description: The framework and its author, so the craft claim is named

source.description: Where it comes from; unverified if we could not check it

fields.description: The questions a reading fills, in order

question.description: What this lens asks of a scene

study-lens.body: What the lens is, in a few lines, and when it tends to explain a story best.

study-engine.description: The distilled method of a studied story, for Crow's Engine tab: what matters about each character, what the world does for the plot, where the scenes come from, why they work, and the recipe to build one. Lives at Studies/<Title>/Engine.md (Kyle, 2026-10-27).
study-engine.body: A lead paragraph with the short answer, then ## sections in the order Crow shows them: The short answer; What matters about each character (one ### per character with - Gift, - Cost, - Pride, - Pattern, - Decoration lines); What the world does for the plot; Where the scenes come from; Why they work; How each scene is built; To build one ourselves; Open questions.

build-premises.description: The premises for a story Kyle builds step by step in Crow, one ## section per premise; Kyle ticks one in Crow and the app writes its title to picked. Lives at Studies/Builds/<Build>/Premises.md (Kyle, 2026-11-05).

picked.description: The title of the premise Kyle ticked in Crow, or empty

lane.description: The exact lane Kyle set for the build, as stacked tags

build-premises.body: A lead line, then one ## section per premise (its title) with - Kind, - Hook, - Readers expect, - Our turn and - The engine lines.

premise-bank.description: Premises Kyle wants kept for good, whatever the current build picks; Crow shows them on its Saved premises page. One note, Studies/Builds/Premise Bank.md (Kyle, 2026-11-05: "create some kind of place where you can store these permanently so that we can always go back to them").
premise-bank.body: A lead line, then one ## section per premise (its title) with - Saved (date and why), - Lane, - Kind, - Hook, - Readers expect, - Our turn and - The engine lines. Add new premises at the end; never remove one without Kyle's word.

build-step.description: One step's work for a story Kyle builds step by step in Crow (tropes, characters, outline...), beside the build's Premises.md. Studies/Builds/<Build>/<Step>.md (Kyle, 2026-11-05).

step.description: The step's name, such as Tropes

build-step.body: What the step found, with sources named, then what the next step takes from it.
